ref-0777cfd4a67d477ca344.text:
PUBLOAD has queried Registry values to identify software using `reg query`.
PUBLOAD has used utilities such as `WinRAR` to archive data prior to exfiltration.
PUBLOAD has used several commands executed in sequence via `cmd` in a short interval to gather software versions including querying Registry keys.
PUBLOAD has used `curl` for data exfiltration over FTP.
PUBLOAD has identified AV products on an infected host using the following command: `WMIC /Node:localhost /Namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 Path AntiVirusProduct Get displayName /Format:List`.
PUBLOAD has identified internet connectivity details through commands such as `tracert -h 5 -4 google.com` and `curl http://myip.ipip.net`.
PUBLOAD has leveraged `wmic logicaldisk get` to map local network drives.
PUBLOAD has used several commands executed in sequence via `cmd` in a short interval to gather information on network connections.
HIUPAN has conducted process discovery to identify the PUBLOAD malware under the process WCBrowserWatcher.exe and will launch it from an install directory if it is not found.
PUBLOAD has obtained information about local networks through the `ipconfig /all` command.
PUBLOAD has collected information on Wi-Fi networks from victim hosts leveraging `netsh wlan show profiles`, `netsh wlan show interface`, and `netsh wlan show`.
PUBLOAD has used several commands executed in sequence via `cmd`.
PUBLOAD has leveraged `tasklist` to gather running services on victim host.
PUBLOAD has used `wmic` to gather information from the victim device.
PUBLOAD has leveraged `curl` for data exfiltration over FTP by uploading RAR archives containing targeted files (.doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .pdf, .ppt, .pptx) to an adversary-owned FTP site.
ref-0777cfd4a67d477ca344.title: Lenart Bermejo, Sunny Lu, Ted Lee. (2024, September 9). Earth Preta Evolves its Attacks with New Malware and Strategies. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.text: Raspberry Robin uses rundll32 execution without any command line parameters to contact command and control infrastructure, such as IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin retrieves its second stage payload in a variety of ways such as through msiexec.exe abuse, or running the curl command to download the payload to the victim's %AppData% folder. Raspberry Robin uses newly-registered domains containing only a few characters for command and controll purposes, such as "v0[.]cx". Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe execution without any command line parameters for command and control requests to IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection. Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe for post-installation communication to command and control infrastructure. Msiexec.exe is executed referencing a remote resource for second-stage payload retrieval and execution. Raspberry Robin uses the Windows utility odbcconf.exe to execute malicious commands, using the regsvr flag to execute DLLs and bypass application control mechanisms that are not monitoring for odbcconf.exe abuse. Raspberry Robin is capable of contacting the TOR network for delivering second-stage payloads. Raspberry Robin has historically been delivered via infected USB drives containing a malicious LNK object masquerading as a legitimate folder. Raspberry Robin uses cmd.exe to read and execute a file stored on an infected USB device as part of initial installation. Raspberry Robin will communicate via HTTP over port 8080 for command and control traffic. Raspberry Robin uses outbound HTTP requests containing victim information for retrieving second stage payloads. Variants of Raspberry Robin can download archive files (such as 7-Zip files) via the victim web browser for second stage execution. Raspberry Robin has historically used infected USB media to spread to new victims. Raspberry Robin will use the legitimate Windows utility fodhelper.exe to run processes at elevated privileges without requiring a User Account Control prompt.
ref-2e5ce0b63b29a50bf2af.title: Lauren Podber and Stef Rand. (2022, May 5). Raspberry Robin gets the worm early. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

ref-440f9bfc1c6db4357d6d.text: Pony has used scripts to delete itself after execution. Pony can download additional files onto the infected system. Pony has sent collected information to the C2 via HTTP POST request. Pony has collected the Service Pack, language, and region information to send to the C2. Pony has used several Windows functions for various purposes. Pony attachments have been delivered via compressed archive files. Pony obfuscates memory flow by adding junk instructions when executing to make analysis more difficult. Pony has used batch scripts to delete itself after execution. Pony has been delivered via spearphishing emails which contained malicious links. Pony has used the NetUserEnum function to enumerate local accounts. Pony has attempted to lure targets into downloading an attached executable (ZIP, RAR, or CAB archives) or document (PDF or other MS Office format). Pony has used a small dictionary of common passwords against a collected list of local accounts. Pony has been delivered via spearphishing attachments. Pony has used the Adobe Reader icon for the downloaded file to look more trustworthy. Pony has attempted to lure targets into clicking links in spoofed emails from legitimate banks. Pony has delayed execution using a built-in function to avoid detection and analysis.
ref-440f9bfc1c6db4357d6d.title: hasherezade. (2016, April 11). No money, but Pony! From a mail to a trojan horse. Retrieved May 21, 2020.

ref-503bc8e0e51652764738.text:
OopsIE uses the SmartAssembly obfuscator to pack an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2.
OopsIE uses the Confuser protector to obfuscate an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2. OopsIE also encodes collected data in hexadecimal format before writing to files on disk and obfuscates strings.
OopsIE compresses collected files with GZipStream before sending them to its C2 server.
OopsIE can upload files from the victim's machine to its C2 server.
OopsIE creates and uses a VBScript as part of its persistent execution.
OopsIE stages the output from command execution and collected files in specific folders before exfiltration.
OopsIE compresses collected files with a simple character replacement scheme before sending them to its C2 server.
OopsIE exfiltrates command output and collected files to its C2 server in 1500-byte blocks.
OopsIE can download files from its C2 server to the victim's machine.
OopsIE uses HTTP for C2 communications.
OopsIE encodes data in hexadecimal format over the C2 channel.
OopsIE creates a scheduled task to run itself every three minutes.
OopsIE uses the command prompt to execute commands on the victim's machine.
OopsIE concatenates then decompresses multiple resources to load an embedded .Net Framework assembly.
ref-503bc8e0e51652764738.title: Lee, B., Falcone, R. (2018, February 23). OopsIE! OilRig Uses ThreeDollars to Deliver New Trojan. Retrieved July 16, 2018.

ref-56ea1a5954fdad966df6.text:
Mini Shai-Hulud has used compromised accounts for Docker Hub and GitHub to publish malicious software packages.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized Python startup hooks to include the .pth import mechanism for execution.
Mini Shai-Hulud has discovered network configuration through the use of system commands to include `ip addr`, and `ip route`.
Mini Shai-Hulud has leveraged commands such as `whoami` to identify the system owner.
Mini Shai-Hulud has compressed collected credentials and data within tar archive files prior to exfiltration.
Mini Shai-Hulud has the ability to decrypt obfuscated payloads.
Mini Shai-Hulud has deleted all artifacts to include gathered credential archives to reduce disk persistence and detection.
ref-56ea1a5954fdad966df6.title: Santos, J. and Navato, J.R. (2026, May 13). Analyzing TeamPCP’s Supply Chain Attacks: Checkmarx KICS and elementary-data in CI/CD Credential Theft. Retrieved July 16, 2026.

ref-6058beb4c72d1e0ba8d7.text: Attor's Blowfish key is encrypted with a public RSA key. Attor's dispatcher disguises itself as a legitimate task (i.e., the task name and description appear legitimate). Attor can obtain application window titles and then determines which windows to perform Screen Capture on. Strings in Attor's components are encrypted with a XOR cipher, using a hardcoded key and the configuration data, log files and plugins are encrypted using a hybrid encryption scheme of Blowfish-OFB combined with RSA. Attor has used FTP protocol for C2 communication. Attor performs the injection by attaching its code into the APC queue using NtQueueApcThread API. Attor has a plugin that enumerates files with specific extensions on all hard disk drives and stores file information in encrypted log files. Attor has used Tor for C2 communication. Attor's dispatcher can execute additional plugins by loading the respective DLLs. Attor has a plugin that collects data stored in the Windows clipboard by using the OpenClipboard and GetClipboardData APIs. Attor's installer plugin can schedule rundll32.exe to load the dispatcher. One of Attor's plugins can collect user credentials via capturing keystrokes and can capture keystrokes pressed within the window of the injected process. Attor's has a plugin that is capable of recording audio using available input sound devices. Attor’s plugin deletes the collected files and log files after exfiltration. Attor has automatically collected data about the compromised system. Attor has a file uploader plugin that automatically exfiltrates the collected data and log files to the C2 server. Attor can download additional plugins, updates and other files. Attor's dispatcher can be executed as a service. Attor's installer plugin can schedule a new task that loads the dispatcher on boot/logon. Attor has a plugin that collects information about inserted storage devices, modems, and phone devices. Attor's dispatcher can establish persistence via adding a Registry key with a logon script HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment "UserInitMprLogonScript" . Attor has manipulated the time of last access to files and registry keys after they have been created or modified. Attor's dispatcher has used CreateProcessW API for execution. Attor encrypts collected data with a custom implementation of Blowfish and RSA ciphers. Attor has staged collected data in a central upload directory prior to exfiltration. Attor's dispatcher can modify the Run registry key. Attor has exfiltrated data over the C2 channel. Attor has encrypted data symmetrically using a randomly generated Blowfish (OFB) key which is encrypted with a public RSA key. Attor can detect whether it is executed in some virtualized or emulated environment by searching for specific artifacts, such as communication with I/O ports and using VM-specific instructions. Attor monitors the free disk space on the system. Attor's dispatcher can inject itself into running processes to gain higher privileges and to evade detection. Attor's has a plugin that captures screenshots of the target applications. Attor's dispatcher can establish persistence by registering a new service. Attor can set attributes of log files and directories to HIDDEN, SYSTEM, ARCHIVE, or a combination of those. Attor has opened the registry and performed query searches.
ref-6058beb4c72d1e0ba8d7.title: Hromcova, Z. (2019, October). AT COMMANDS, TOR-BASED COMMUNICATIONS: MEET ATTOR, A FANTASY CREATURE AND ALSO A SPY PLATFORM. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

ref-772feec56b85283e984b.text:
Vidar has been distributed via malicious advertisements when users searched for “Notepad++.”
Vidar has compiled collected data into a randomly generated directory in the ProgramData folder.
Vidar has downloaded additional binaries from the C2 server such as sqlx[1].dll, a sqlite3 binary for data harvesting and exfiltration. Vidar has also ownloaded get.zip, an archive containing several DLL libraries that extracted data from applications and browsers.
Vidar has used process hollowing to inject itself into an AppLaunch.exe process.
Vidar has used a hidden directory in the ProgramData directory to store collected data.
Vidar has set the Registry value associated with User Access Control (UAC) (i.e. `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA`) to `0`, which disabled UAC.
Vidar has used Telegram and Steam dead drop resolvers to recover its C2 domain.
Vidar has used the function `TerminateProcess` to terminate processes. Vidar has forcefully terminated a process named Devil.exe using the command `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe” /c taskkill /im Devil.exe /f`.
Vidar has used HTTP/HTTPS to retrieve and send data and beacons.
Vidar has self-deleted its initial executable to operate in memory. Vidar has deleted collected data after exfiltration. Vidar has also deleted the file Malware.exe and all .dll files in the ProgramData folder using the command `del /f /q “C:\Users\MalWorkstation\Desktop\Malware.exe” & del C:\ProgramData\*.dll`.
Vidar has bypassed UAC by setting the Registry value `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA` to `0`, which disabled UAC.
Vidar has used PowerShell commands to modify Windows Defender’s list of excluded file extensions.
Vidar has waited for six seconds using the command `timeout /t 6`.
Vidar has collected browser history from the victim machine.
ref-772feec56b85283e984b.title: Khadgi, N. (n.d.). A Comprehensive Overview on Stealer Malware Families. Retrieved August 25, 2026.

ref-78775720f32010aed47b.text:
XLoader can collect data stored in the victim's clipboard.
XLoader can use an AutoIT script to decrypt a payload file, load it into victim memory, then execute it on the victim machine.
XLoader can capture keystrokes from the victim machine.
XLoader can conduct form grabbing, steal cookies, and extract data from HTTP sessions.
XLoader uses HTTP and HTTPS for command and control communication.
XLoader uses XOR and RC4 algorithms to decrypt payloads and functions. XLoader can be distributed as a self-extracting RAR archive that launches an AutoIT loader.
XLoader establishes persistence by copying its executable in a subdirectory of `%APPDATA%` or `%PROGRAMFILES%`, and then modifies Windows Registry Run keys or policies keys to execute the executable on system start.
XLoader can capture screenshots on compromised hosts.
XLoader uses anti-debugging mechanisms such as calling `NtQueryInformationProcess` with `InfoClass=7`, referencing `ProcessDebugPort`, to determine if it is being analyzed.
XLoader performs timing checks using the Read-Time Stamp Counter (RDTSC) instruction on the victim CPU.
XLoader can collect credentials stored in email clients.
XLoader can initiate a system reboot or shutdown.
XLoader can capture web session cookies and session information from victim browsers.
XLoader has been delivered as a phishing attachment, including PDFs with embedded links, Word and Excel files, and various archive files (ZIP, RAR, ACE, and ISOs) containing EXE payloads.
XLoader can gather credentials from several web browsers.
ref-78775720f32010aed47b.title: Nart Villeneuve, Randi Eitzman, Sandor Nemes & Tyler Dean, Google Cloud. (2017, October 5). Significant FormBook Distribution Campaigns Impacting the U.S. and South Korea. Retrieved March 11, 2025.

ref-8a67235d527361450af3.text:
PowerLess has the ability to exfiltrate data, including Chrome and Edge browser database files, from compromised machines.
PowerLess can use a module to log keystrokes.
PowerLess can use base64 and AES ECB decryption prior to execution of downloaded modules.
PowerLess can encrypt browser database files prior to exfiltration.
PowerLess is written in and executed via PowerShell without using powershell.exe.
PowerLess can use an encrypted channel for C2 communications.
PowerLess can stage stolen browser data in `C:\\Windows\\Temp\\cup.tmp` and keylogger data in `C:\\Windows\\Temp\\Report.06E17A5A-7325-4325-8E5D-E172EBA7FC5BK`.
PowerLess can download additional payloads to a compromised host.
PowerLess has a browser info stealer module that can read Chrome and Edge browser database files.
ref-8a67235d527361450af3.title: Cybereason Nocturnus. (2022, February 1). PowerLess Trojan: Iranian APT Phosphorus Adds New PowerShell Backdoor for Espionage. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

ref-9386b4b28d4383e6cc39.text:
Micropsia can perform microphone recording.
Micropsia can perform a recursive directory listing for all volume drives available on the victim's machine and can also fetch specific files by their paths.
Micropsia has keylogging capabilities.
Micropsia creates a RAR archive based on collected files on the victim's machine.
Micropsia executes an RAR tool to recursively archive files based on a predefined list of file extensions (*.xls, *.xlsx, *.csv, *.odt, *.doc, *.docx, *.ppt, *.pptx, *.pdf, *.mdb, *.accdb, *.accde, *.txt).
Micropsia creates a new hidden directory to store all components' outputs in a dedicated sub-folder for each.
Micropsia takes screenshots every 90 seconds by calling the Gdi32.BitBlt API.
Micropsia creates a command-line shell using cmd.exe.
ref-9386b4b28d4383e6cc39.title: Tsarfaty, Y. (2018, July 25). Micropsia Malware. Retrieved November 13, 2018.

ref-aabc1e711642e2f82759.text: Dtrack has used process hollowing shellcode to target a predefined list of processes from %SYSTEM32%. Dtrack has used a dropper that embeds an encrypted payload as extra data. Dtrack can collect network and active connection information. Dtrack can retrieve browser history. Dtrack can collect the host's IP addresses using the ipconfig command. Dtrack’s dropper contains a keylogging executable. Dtrack’s RAT makes a persistent target file with auto execution on the host start. Dtrack can remove its persistence and delete itself. Dtrack can list files on available disk volumes. Dtrack’s dropper can list all running processes. Dtrack can save collected data to disk, different file formats, and network shares. Dtrack has used a decryption routine that is part of an executable physical patch. Dtrack can collect the victim's computer name, hostname and adapter information to create a unique identifier. Dtrack packs collected data into a password protected archive. Dtrack’s can download and upload a file to the victim’s computer.
ref-aabc1e711642e2f82759.title: Konstantin Zykov. (2019, September 23). Hello! My name is Dtrack. Retrieved January 20, 2021.

ref-ad939f4a8629b3e6897a.text: Epic gathers information on local group names. Epic compresses the collected data with bzip2 before sending it to the C2 server. Epic uses the tasklist /v command to obtain a list of processes. Epic collects the user name from the victim’s machine. Epic encrypts collected data using a public key framework before sending it over the C2 channel. Some variants encrypt the collected data with AES and encode it with base64 before transmitting it to the C2 server. Epic collects the OS version, hardware information, computer name, available system memory status, and system and user language settings. Epic uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications. Epic has a command to delete a file from the machine. Epic collects disk space information. Epic gathers a list of all user accounts, privilege classes, and time of last logon. Epic recursively searches for all .doc files on the system and collects a directory listing of the Desktop, %TEMP%, and %WINDOWS%\Temp directories. Epic uses the net use, net session, and netstat commands to gather information on network connections.
ref-ad939f4a8629b3e6897a.title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2014, August 06). The Epic Turla Operation: Solving some of the mysteries of Snake/Uroboros. Retrieved November 7, 2018.

ref-bf8edefd52af684f024f.text:
InvisibleFerret has utilized a PowerShell script created in the victim’s home directory named “conf.ps1” that is used to modify configuration files for AnyDesk remote services.
InvisibleFerret has utilized the command `ssh_zcp` to exfiltrate data from browser extensions and password managers via Telegram and FTP.
BeaverTail has collected keys stored for Solana stored in `.config/solana/id.json` and other login details associated with macOS within `/Library/Keychains/login.keychain` or for Linux within `/.local/share/keyrings`.
InvisibleFerret has staged data in consolidated folders prior to exfiltration.
BeaverTail has obtained and sent the current timestamp associated with the victim device to C2.
InvisibleFerret has used 7zip, RAR and zip files to archive collected data for exfiltration.
BeaverTail has identified .ldb and .log files stored in browser extension directories for collection and exfiltration.
InvisibleFerret has executed Python instances of the browser module “.n2/bow” utilizing the `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` process creation flag.
InvisibleFerret has collected data utilizing a script that contained a list of excluded files and directory names and naming patterns of interest such as environment and configuration files, documents, spreadsheets, and other files that contained the words secret, wallet, private, and password.
InvisibleFerret has leveraged Telegram chat to upload stolen data using the Telegram API with a bot token.
InvisibleFerret has decoded XOR-encrypted and Base-64-encoded payloads prior to execution.
BeaverTail has added junk data or a dummy character prepended to a string to hamper decoding attempts.
ref-bf8edefd52af684f024f.title: Matej Havranek. (2025, February 20). DeceptiveDevelopment targets freelance developers. Retrieved October 17, 2025.

ref-d9794d16b217472dc38d.text:
MiniFast has collected the username on targeted systems.
MiniFast has decoded Base64-encoded tasks from the C2.
MiniFast has the ability to upload files over C2 communications.
MiniFast has blended into network traffic by mimicking a Chrome browser using the following User-Agent string: `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`.
MiniFast has encoded C2 instructions with Base64.
MiniFast has the ability to delete files and directories.
MiniFast has leveraged valid digital signatures from SSL[.]com to appear legitimate.
MiniFast has collected the victim's username, hostname and domain information.
MiniFast has listed files and folders within a specified directory.
MiniFast has enumerated logical drives on impacted devices.
MiniFast has the ability to terminate a process using its PID.
MiniFast has executed commands using `cmd.exe`.
MiniFast has collected data from local files and directories on the victim device.
MiniFast has created scheduled tasks using the name “WindowsSecurityUpdate.”
MiniFast has the ability to move data within the victim machine.
MiniFast has utilized HTTP POST, GET and PUT requests for communications with the C2.
MiniFast has been delivered within a malicious zip file.
MiniFast has the ability to archive files and directories using ZIP.
MiniFast has the ability to download additional files from C2.
MiniFast has the ability to check running processes and has returned process names and their PIDs. MiniFast has also checked its relative parent process.
MiniFast has the ability to execute a process with elevated privileges using `runas`.
ref-d9794d16b217472dc38d.title: Check Point. (2026, May 22). Fast and Furious – Nimbus Manticore Operations During the Iranian Conflict. Retrieved September 23, 2026.

ref-e269bf3a244a2d200330.text:
Line Runner used CVE-2024-20353 to trigger victim devices to reboot, in the process unzipping and installing the Line Dancer payload.
Line Dancer can gather system configuration information by running the native `show configuration` command.
Line Runner intercepts HTTP requests to the victim Cisco ASA, looking for a request with a 32-character, victim dependent parameter. If that parameter matches a value in the malware, a contained payload is then written to a Lua script and executed.
Line Dancer can execute native commands in networking device command line interfaces.
Line Dancer can hook both the crash dump process and the Autehntication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) functions on compromised machines to evade forensic analysis and authentication mechanisms.
Line Dancer exfiltrates collected data via command and control channels.
Line Runner utilizes HTTP to retrieve and exfiltrate information staged using Line Dancer.
Line Runner utilizes an HTTP-based Lua backdoor on victim machines.
Line Dancer can modify the crash dump process on infected machines to skip crash dump generation and proceed directly to device reboot for both persistence and forensic evasion purposes.
Line Dancer uses HTTP POST requests to interact with compromised devices.
Line Runner utilizes Lua scripts for command execution.
Line Dancer can create and exfiltrate packet captures from compromised environments.
Line Runner removes its initial ZIP delivery archive after processing the enclosed LUA script.
Line Dancer can disable syslog on compromised devices.
Line Runner uses a ZIP payload that is automatically extracted with its contents, a LUA script, executed for initial execution via CVE-2024-20359.
ref-e269bf3a244a2d200330.title: Cisco Talos. (2024, April 24). ArcaneDoor - New espionage-focused campaign found targeting perimeter network devices. Retrieved January 6, 2025.

ref-ebf062c3a671412fc496.text: Machete has scanned and looked for cryptographic keys and certificate file extensions. Machete can download additional files for execution on the victim’s machine. Machete sends stolen data to the C2 server every 10 minutes. Machete’s downloaded data is decrypted using AES. Machete retrieves the user profile data (e.g., browsers) from Chrome and Firefox browsers. Machete's collected data is encrypted with AES before exfiltration. Machete has a component to check for running processes to look for web browsers. Machete detects the insertion of new devices by listening for the WM_DEVICECHANGE window message. Machete renamed task names to masquerade as legitimate Google Chrome, Java, Dropbox, Adobe Reader and Python tasks. Machete uses the netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid and netsh wlan show interfaces commands to list all nearby WiFi networks and connected interfaces. Machete's collected data is exfiltrated over the same channel used for C2. Machete has used AES to exfiltrate documents. Machete has sent data over HTTP if FTP failed, and has also used a fallback server. Machete’s collected files are exfiltrated automatically to remote servers. Once a file is uploaded, Machete will delete it from the machine. Machete collects stored credentials from several web browsers. Machete has the capability to exfiltrate stolen data to a hidden folder on a removable drive. Machete searches the File system for files of interest. Machete has been packed with NSIS. Machete saves the window names. Machete stores zipped files with profile data from installed web browsers. Machete collects the hostname of the target computer.
ref-ebf062c3a671412fc496.title: ESET. (2019, July). MACHETE JUST GOT SHARPER Venezuelan government institutions under attack. Retrieved September 13, 2019.
